items.prompt: What is the merge base?
choices: The last commit both branches share
The newest commit on the branch you are on
The first commit in the repository
items.explanation: The merge base is the shared ancestor: where the two histories split.

items.prompt: A three-way merge compares the merge base against what?
choices: Only the branch you are on
items.explanation: Three-way means base, ours, and theirs are all used.

items.prompt: Why does git need the merge base at all?
choices: To make the merge run faster
To count how many commits each side has
items.explanation: Without the base, a difference between two files cannot be credited to either person.

items.prompt: In the two-photos analogy, the merge base is...
choices: The original photo before any edits
The nicer of the two edited photos
A copy of the most recent edit
items.explanation: The original is what lets you see what each edit actually changed.

items.prompt: How many versions of the file does a three-way merge look at?
items.explanation: Base, ours, and theirs.

items.prompt: Comparing the base to Alex's branch tells git...
items.explanation: Base to Alex is Alex's change list only.

items.prompt: Two files differ on one line and git has no base. What does it know?
items.explanation: A bare difference carries no information about who made it.

items.prompt: Where does the merge base sit in history?
choices: At the tip of the longer branch
items.explanation: It is the point where they last agreed.

items.prompt: Branch A and branch B both start from commit C1. A then gets two more commits, B gets one. What is the merge base?
choices: The tip commit of branch A
The tip commit of branch B
The commit made right after the merge completes
items.explanation: The shared ancestor is where histories split, not either tip, so it stays C1 however many commits each side adds.
items.reference:
Three versions, not two
📍 base: the shared starting commit
🌿 Alex's branch: base plus Alex's edits
🌿 Sam's branch: base plus Sam's edits
Why: comparing each branch to the base shows who changed what; two files alone only show that they differ.
items.learnMore:
The base is the missing witness

Two differing files cannot say which side made a change. The merge base is the shared before-picture that turns a vague difference into two clear change lists.

Common mistake

Thinking the merge base is the newest commit on either branch. It is the last commit they have in common.
items.reflection: Two people edit copies of the same shared document offline. What would you need to keep from before they started, in order to combine their edits without guessing?

items.prompt: A line reads 5 in the base, 5 on Alex's branch, and 6 on Sam's. What does having the base add compared with just seeing the two branches differ?
choices: It shows both changed it, so the line conflicts
It shows only Sam changed it, so 6 is the safe result
It shows Alex changed it, so 5 is the safe result
It shows neither side changed it, so the line is left untouched
items.explanation: With the base, an unchanged side is recognised: Alex's 5 equals the base, so the only edit is Sam's.

items.prompt: Alex and Sam edit different lines of one file. What happens?
choices: Git keeps only the later change
items.explanation: Non-overlapping edits are combined automatically.

items.prompt: Both edit the same line to different content. What happens?
items.explanation: Git cannot guess which is right, so it stops.

items.prompt: Does editing the same file mean a conflict?
items.explanation: The file is not the unit; the line is.

items.prompt: When a conflict appears, did git destroy anyone's work?
choices: No, both versions are in the file
Yes, the older commit is deleted
items.explanation: Git writes both sides into the file for you to settle.

items.prompt: Which three marker lines show a conflict?
choices: Start, middle divider, and end markers
items.explanation: The markers wrap both versions in the file itself.

items.prompt: A conflict means git...
items.explanation: It is a request for a human decision.

items.prompt: First step after git reports a conflict?
choices: Open the file and read both sides
items.explanation: You need to see what each side wanted.

items.prompt: Which pair of edits merges with no help?
choices: Both delete the same line and edit it differently
Both rewrite the same line to different values
One adds a guard, one changes a constant elsewhere
items.explanation: Edits on different lines do not collide.

items.prompt: A file has 3 lines. Alex edits line 1, Sam edits line 3. What does git do?
choices: Flags a conflict because the file is shared
Keeps only the first edit it sees
Conflicts at both lines, since the file has two edits
items.explanation: The edits touch different lines, so neither collides; both apply.
items.reference:
Auto-merge or conflict?
✅ different lines edited → combined automatically
⚠️ same line, different content → conflict
🟰 same line, same content → no conflict
Why: what matters is whether the exact lines collide, not whether both people touched the file.
items.learnMore:
A conflict is git declining to guess

Nothing is lost when a merge stops. Both versions are written into the file so a person can choose. Most merges never reach this point.

Common mistake

Believing any two edits to one file conflict. Only collisions on the same lines do.
items.reflection: Two friends plan a trip in one shared document. Which kinds of simultaneous edits would merge peacefully, and which would force a conversation?

items.prompt: On line 2, the base says `a`. Alex changes it to `b`, Sam changes it to `c`. What results?
choices: Git picks `b` because Alex committed first
A conflict that a person must settle
Git keeps the base text because the edits cancel out
items.explanation: Both changed the same line differently, so there is no safe automatic choice.

items.prompt: Neither side changed a line. What does git keep?
items.explanation: No change from either side means the base stands.

items.prompt: Only ours changed the line. Which is kept?
items.explanation: The other side did not change it, so ours wins.

items.prompt: Only theirs changed the line. Which is kept?
items.explanation: Same rule mirrored.

items.prompt: Both sides changed the line to different content.
items.explanation: A real disagreement is the only thing a person must settle.

items.prompt: Both sides changed the line to the same new content.
items.explanation: They agree; there is nothing to ask.

items.prompt: How many yes/no questions does git ask about each line?
choices: Two: changed on ours? changed on theirs?
Three: one per branch and one for base
items.explanation: Those two answers cover every case.

items.prompt: In `git merge alex-branch` run by Sam, who is ours?
choices: Sam's branch, the one you are on
items.explanation: Ours is the checked-out branch.

items.prompt: In that merge, who is theirs?
choices: Alex's branch, the one being merged in
items.explanation: Theirs is the branch you name in the command.

items.prompt: A line is `a` in the base, `a` in ours, and `b` in theirs. What is the result?
choices: A conflict, because the versions differ
`a`, because the base wins unless both sides agree
items.explanation: Ours equals the base, so only theirs made an edit and it applies.
items.reference:
Per-line decision
➖ neither changed → keep base
🔹 one side changed → take that side
🟰 both changed, same result → take it
💥 both changed, different → conflict
Why: git asks two questions for every line, changed on ours? changed on theirs?, and the answers decide the outcome.
items.learnMore:
Changed means different from the base

A side counts as having changed a line only if its version differs from the base's. A side whose line equals the base has not spoken, so the other side wins automatically.

Common mistake

Comparing ours to theirs directly. The base is the reference for both.
items.reflection: When two people disagree about a recipe, it helps to know which of them actually changed something from the original. Where else does knowing the 'original' turn an apparent standoff into an easy call?

items.prompt: Why do short-lived branches conflict less?
choices: Less time for edits to overlap
Git skips checks on short branches
items.explanation: Less divergence means fewer shared lines edited.

items.prompt: Conflict risk mostly grows with...
choices: The number of files in the repo
items.explanation: Overlap on the same lines is the real driver.

items.prompt: main has not moved since feature branched off. feature has 3 new commits. What does merging feature into main do?
choices: Creates a merge commit with three parents
Opens a conflict for each commit
Rebases feature onto main and rewrites its history
Fast-forwards main; no merge commit and no conflict possible
items.explanation: With main untouched, one change list is empty, so the pointer slides forward.
items.reference:
One comparison, three outcomes
🟩 different lines → auto-merge
🟥 same line, different content → conflict
⏩ one side never moved → fast-forward
Why: the same three-way comparison produces all of them; they differ only in what it finds.
items.learnMore:
Fast-forward is the empty case

If the receiving branch has made no commits since the split, one change list is empty and there is nothing to reconcile. Git moves the pointer and creates no merge commit.

Common mistake

Assuming every merge makes a merge commit. A fast-forward does not.

items.prompt: Sam is on main and runs `git merge alex-branch`. The block shows `0.0825` first and `0.075` second. Which value is Alex's?
choices: The merge base's, shown in the middle
items.explanation: The first half is the current branch (Sam), the second is the branch merged in (Alex).
items.reference:
Anatomy of a marker block
🔼 first half (after the opening marker): ours, the branch you are on
🔽 second half (before the closing marker): theirs, the branch merged in
🧹 outside the markers: already merged, leave alone
Why: the markers are a question git left in the file; resolving means writing the final lines, deleting the markers, then checking it works.
items.learnMore:
Resolve, then prove

Choosing a side or combining both fixes the file's shape. Running tests or a manual check is what confirms the choice was right. `git add` only records that you consider the file settled.

Common mistake

Treating 'no markers left' as 'correct'. Git cannot check your decision.
items.reflection: Imagine two editors both rewrote the same paragraph and the document now shows both. How would you decide the final wording, and how would you know the result still reads right?

items.prompt: Alex renames `getTotal` to `calcTotal` everywhere in file A. Sam adds a call to `getTotal` in file B. Git merges with no conflict. What is true?
choices: The build can break even though git was satisfied

items.explanation: Different files and lines never collide, but the combined code calls a name that no longer exists.
items.reference:
What lines can't tell you
🔤 git sees lines, not meaning
🧩 a clean merge can still be broken code
🧪 tests on the merged result are the safety net
Why: no line collided does not mean the program works; only running it on the merged result shows that.
items.learnMore:
Semantic conflicts

Two changes that are each valid can be wrong together, for example a rename on one branch and a new use of the old name on the other. Git sees different lines and merges cleanly.

Common mistake

Equating 'no conflicts reported' with 'safe to ship'.
items.reflection: Two people tidy a shared spreadsheet: one renames a column, the other adds a formula using the old name. Nothing overlapped, yet it breaks. Where in your own work could independent changes quietly fail together?

items.reference:
What lines can't tell you
🔤 git sees lines, not meaning
🧩 a clean merge can still be broken code
🧪 tests on the merged result are the safety net
Why: no line collided does not mean the program works; only running it on the merged result shows that.
items.learnMore:
Semantic conflicts

Two changes that are each valid can be wrong together, for example a rename on one branch and a new use of the old name on the other. Git sees different lines and merges cleanly.

Common mistake

Equating 'no conflicts reported' with 'safe to ship'.
items.reflection: Two people tidy a shared spreadsheet: one renames a column, the other adds a formula using the old name. Nothing overlapped, yet it breaks. Where in your own work could independent changes quietly fail together?
